references.text: The preceding verse ([ref:Luk 11:47|Luke 11:47]) describes how they build tombs over the prophets whom their fathers killed – precisely that action which verse 48 points back to as evidence that they are witnesses and consent to their fathers' deeds.

In [ref:Matt 23:29-32|Matthew 23:29-32] we find the parallel where Jesus says they build tombs over the prophets and adorn the graves of the righteous, thereby testifying against themselves that they are children of those who killed the prophets – they fill up their fathers' measure.

Stephen's speech in [ref:Apg 7:51-52|Acts 7:51-52] reflects the same theme: the fathers persecuted and killed the prophets who proclaimed the coming of the Righteous One, and now their descendants have betrayed and killed him.
In [ref:Apg 22:20|Acts 22:20] Paul uses the word "συνευδοκῶν" (consent) regarding his own role at Stephen's death – the same word used in Luke 11:48 about consenting to the fathers' deeds.

In [ref:Rom 1:32|Romans 1:32] the word "συνευδοκοῦσιν" is used concerning those who not only do evil themselves but also give their consent to those who do it – the same principle of shared responsibility through consent.

[ref:2 Krøn 36:15-16|2 Chronicles 36:15-16] describes how God again and again sent his messengers to the people, but they mocked God's envoys, despised his words and scoffed at his prophets – the background for Jesus' accusation about the fathers killing the prophets.

[ref:Neh 9:26|Nehemiah 9:26] confesses that the fathers were disobedient and rebelled, cast God's law behind their backs and killed the prophets who testified against them – a historical confirmation of what Jesus refers to.

In [ref:Jer 2:30|Jeremiah 2:30] the Lord says the sword devoured the prophets "like a destroying lion" – yet another example that Israel's fathers killed the prophets, which forms the basis for Jesus' words in this verse.

In [ref:1 Tess 2:14-15|1 Thessalonians 2:14-15] Paul writes that the Jews killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets – a continuation of the theme of persecution of God's messengers through the generations.
